property_summary: For any caller and any msg.value, the reference contract only accepts calls that send exactly 10 ether (calls with other values revert), so pastBlockTime is only updated when msg.value == 10 ether — the mutant that requires 1 ether instead will accept different msg.value and thus allow pastBlockTime updates for values that should be rejected by the reference.

For every call to the contract's fallback, the reference C only accepts (does not revert) when msg.value == 10 ether, so pastBlockTime can only be updated by calls sending exactly 10 ether; the mutant accepts 1 ether so it will accept some values that the reference rejects, breaking the universal rule.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether, the reference contract always requires the block timestamp to strictly increase (block.timestamp > pastBlockTime) so two successful calls in the same block cannot both update pastBlockTime — the mutant using >= allows a second call in the same block to succeed and thus can change c.pastBlockTime (and trigger a transfer) whereas the reference never lets a second same-block call pass the timestamp check.

For any caller and any timestamp, the reference contract never allows two successful payable fallback calls in the same block to both update pastBlockTime (the second call in the same block must revert due to block.timestamp > pastBlockTime); the mutant using >= can allow a second call in the same block to succeed and thus break this invariant.

After any successful fallback call sending exactly 10 ether from any caller at a strictly later timestamp than pastBlockTime, the contract's pastBlockTime equals the block.timestamp (the reference stores timestamp; the mutant storing block.number can make pastBlockTime differ), so the mutant can produce a mismatch where pastBlockTime != block.timestamp.

For any successful payable fallback call of exactly 10 ether made at a strictly later block.timestamp than the stored pastBlockTime, the contract updates pastBlockTime to the current block.timestamp; the mutant that writes block.number instead will cause pastBlockTime != block.timestamp for some inputs (e.g., when block.number != block.timestamp), breaking this invariant.

For every successful payable fallback call sending exactly 10 ether at a strictly later block.timestamp than the stored pastBlockTime, the contract records pastBlockTime equal to the current block.timestamp; the mutant that writes block.number instead will make pastBlockTime != block.timestamp for some inputs (when block.number != block.timestamp).

For any call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether, the reference contract always advances pastBlockTime to a strictly greater timestamp than its previous value (so two consecutive successful fallback calls cannot leave pastBlockTime unchanged), while the mutant that removes the timestamp ordering allows a second call in the same block.timestamp to overwrite pastBlockTime and thus can make pastBlockTime equal to its prior value after the call sequence.

Invariant: any successful call to fallback with msg.value == 10 ether strictly increases C.pastBlockTime (so pastBlockTime after the call is greater than before); the mutant removing the require allows calling fallback twice in the same block.timestamp so pastBlockTime can remain equal to its previous value, violating the invariant.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to fallback, the reference C never allows pastBlockTime to decrease or stay the same across two consecutive successful fallback calls made from the same external account without advancing block.timestamp (i.e., performing two calls with the same block.timestamp cannot both succeed under the reference because the second call requires block.timestamp > pastBlockTime), whereas the mutant (which removes the timestamp ordering require) can accept a second call at the same block.timestamp and thus leave pastBlockTime unchanged after the second call — so the rule: after two successive fallback calls from the same caller performed at the same block.timestamp with msg.value == 10 ether, the reference either reverts on the second call (so the second call does not complete) or, if it completes, pastBlockTime strictly increases; the mutant can complete both calls and have pastBlockTime equal to its prior value.

For any caller sending exactly 10 ether to C.fallback, the reference contract enforces that the call will only succeed if block.timestamp is strictly greater than the stored pastBlockTime (so a call that succeeds guarantees pastBlockTime increases), whereas the mutant removes that ordering check and therefore can accept a call at the same timestamp and leave pastBlockTime unchanged, violating this rule.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether at a strictly later timestamp, the reference contract only pays out the full balance when block.number % 15 == 0; the mutant instead pays out on block.number % 10 == 0, so there exist fuzzed block numbers where the reference retains balance but the mutant drains it.

For any call to fallback sending exactly 10 ether at a strictly increasing timestamp, the reference C never empties its balance on blocks where block.number % 15 != 0 (i.e. it only transfers the full balance when block.number % 15 == 0); the mutant transfers on block.number % 10 == 0 instead, so there exist blocks where the mutant drains the contract but the reference does not.

For every call to fallback that sends exactly 10 ether and occurs at a strictly later timestamp, the reference contract only transfers its full balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0 (so on other blocks the contract's balance remains >0), whereas the mutant transfers on block.number % 10 == 0 and therefore can drain the contract on some blocks where the reference would not.

For any caller and block state where C.fallback accepts the call (msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime), the reference contract always transfers the entire contract balance to the caller when block.number % 15 == 0, so after the call address(c).balance == 0; the mutant that transfers only 1 ether violates this by leaving a nonzero contract balance for some inputs.

For any caller and timestamp where the fallback accepts the call (msg.value == 10 ether and block.timestamp > pastBlockTime), if the call happens on a block with number divisible by 15 then the correct contract forwards its entire balance leaving address(c).balance == 0, while the mutant that transfers only 1 ether can leave a nonzero balance — so the rule is: after such a successful fallback on block % 15 == 0, address(c).balance == 0; the mutant violates this for some inputs.
